title: FX-swap-implied USD rate from EUR — Ando (2012) decomposition
source: Ando (2012), 'Recent developments in US dollar funding costs through FX swaps' (Bank of Japan Review) — Box: Arbitrage Conditions for FX Swaps
problem:
Apply Ando's decomposition of the FX-swap-implied USD rate from EUR.

**Observed rates (3M tenor):**

| Rate | Value |
|---|---:|
| USD OIS | 4.20% |
| USD LIBOR | 4.55% |
| EUR OIS | 3.30% |
| EUR LIBOR | 3.45% |
| Basis residual α | +0.20% |

Compute (a) the FX-swap-implied USD rate from EUR; (b) the USD and EUR LIBOR-OIS spreads; (c) the no-arbitrage upper bound and how much the observed rate exceeds it.
keyFormulas: FX-swap-implied USD rate from EUR = USD OIS + (USD LIBOR − USD OIS) + (EUR LIBOR − EUR OIS) + α
No-arbitrage range: USD OIS ≤ FX-swap-implied USD rate ≤ USD LIBOR + (EUR LIBOR − EUR OIS)
α = the residual that captures stress beyond unsecured-market counterparty risk

parts.prompt: (a) Compute the FX-swap-implied USD rate from EUR.
working: FX-swap-implied USD rate = USD OIS + USD LIBOR-OIS + EUR LIBOR-OIS + α

parts.prompt: (b) Compute the USD and EUR LIBOR-OIS spreads.
parts.answer: USD LIBOR-OIS = 35 bp · EUR LIBOR-OIS = 15 bp
working: Per Ando: each LIBOR-OIS spread isolates 'concern over counterparty risk observed in the unsecured markets' for that currency.

parts.prompt: (c) Compute the no-arbitrage upper bound and the excess of the implied rate over it.
working: No-arb upper bound = USD LIBOR + (EUR LIBOR − EUR OIS) = 4.55% + 0.15% = **4.70%**.
Implied 4.90% exceeds the bound by **0.20% = 20 bp**, exactly equal to α.
Per Ando: when α > 0, 'demand for funding through the FX swap was strong' — i.e. dollar funding stress beyond what unsecured-market spreads alone explain.

intuition: The Ando identity makes the FX-swap-implied USD rate exactly attributable to four observable components, with α isolating the residual dollar-funding stress. When all three known components (USD OIS, the two LIBOR-OIS spreads) are pinned down, α IS the cross-currency basis dislocation. A positive α here means synthetic USD via the FX swap is more expensive than CIP + unsecured-market premia would justify — the canonical 2008 and March 2020 pattern.

title: Cross-currency basis cost on a EUR/USD CCBS hedge
source: Coffey, Kos & Verdelhan (2009), 'The global financial crisis and offshore dollar markets' + Lecture 9 (CCBS mechanics)
problem:
A European bank funds USD assets via a 5-year EUR/USD cross-currency basis swap. The basis on the EUR leg is **−35 bp** (i.e. the bank receives EURIBOR − 35 bp / pays USD LIBOR flat).

• Notional: **EUR 100m** (= **USD 110m** at spot 1.10 USD/EUR).
• Tenor: 5 years.

Compute (a) the annualised cost of the basis in EUR; (b) in USD; (c) the 5-year total simple cost; (d) the 5-year PV of the cost stream at a 4% discount rate.
keyFormulas: Annual basis cost = Notional × |basis spread|
PV of an annuity = C × [1 − (1+r)^(−n)] / r

parts.prompt: (b) Annualised basis cost in USD at spot 1.10.
working: Equivalently, 35 bp on EUR notional ≈ 35 bp on USD notional (basis is in spread units, near-invariant to currency conversion at small spreads).

parts.prompt: (c) 5-year total simple cost (no discounting), in EUR.
(d) 5-year PV of the cost stream at a 4% discount rate, in EUR.

intuition: A persistent negative basis is a direct deadweight cost on banks that fund foreign-currency assets via swaps. Coffey, Kos & Verdelhan (2009) document the post-Lehman EUR/USD basis blowing out to several hundred bp at peak — meaning tens of basis points of structural funding cost on every dollar borrowed synthetically by a non-US bank, repaid year after year, exactly when capital is scarce.

title: March 2020 NBFI: VM call + over-hedge rebalancing
source: Alstadheim, Nordal, Syrstad et al. (Norges Bank guest lecture 2026), 'Bond market fire sales and turbulence in the Norwegian FX market in March 2020'
problem:
A Norwegian NBFI holds **USD 100m** of US equities, fully hedged via an FX swap that locks the forward sell-rate at **9.50 NOK/USD**. The swap is short-USD / long-NOK.

During 16–20 March 2020:
• NOK depreciates: spot rises from **9.50 → 11.30 NOK/USD**.
• US equity portfolio falls **30%** in USD terms: USD 100m → USD 70m.

Compute (a) the NOK variation-margin (VM) call from the FX swap MtM move; (b) the spot NOK selling required to right-size the over-sized hedge; (c) total NOK liquidity demand from this single firm.
keyFormulas: MtM on a short-USD forward = (S_now − F_lock) × USD notional, expressed in NOK
Over-hedge USD = original USD notional − new asset USD value
Spot NOK sold to right-size = over-hedge USD × current spot

parts.prompt: (a) Variation margin call from MtM on the FX swap.
working: NBFI is short USD forward at F = 9.50. As spot rises to 11.30, the swap is in the money for the counterparty, out of the money for the NBFI.
MtM loss to NBFI = (S_now − F_lock) × USD notional = (11.30 − 9.50) × 100,000,000 = **180,000,000 NOK** (±0.5m).
Daily VM under EMIR/BCBS-IOSCO: NBFI must wire 180m NOK in cash collateral to the counterparty.
Channel (a) per Alstadheim: NBFIs raise this NOK by selling Norwegian bonds → bond risk premiums spike to 75 / 225 / 250 bp on 5y covered / senior bank / corporate.

parts.prompt: (b) Spot NOK selling required to right-size the over-sized hedge.
working: USD asset value falls to USD 70m; hedge still locked at USD 100m → over-hedge of USD 30m.
To reduce hedge to USD 70m, NBFI buys USD 30m and sells NOK at the new spot 11.30.
Channel (b) per Alstadheim: aggregate NBFI sector sold ~25 bn NOK net during the crisis weeks via this rebalancing channel.

parts.prompt: (c) Total NOK liquidity demand from this single firm.
working: Total = VM cash + spot NOK sold = 180m + 339m = **519,000,000 NOK** (±1m).
Note the channels stress different markets: VM stresses the NOK bond market (forced sales for cash); rebalancing stresses the spot FX market (NOK selling pressure).

intuition: The two channels operate independently and stack. A single mid-sized Norwegian NBFI can generate half a billion NOK of liquidity demand on a USD 100m position — the bond-market and FX-market dislocations of March 2020 are the aggregation of this dynamic across the sector. The textbook lesson: derivative hedges convert price risk into liquidity risk (Set 1 question on hedging) and that liquidity risk is what actually breaks markets in stress.

title: LIBOR-OIS arithmetic — α exceeds the no-arbitrage bound
source: Ando (2012), Bank of Japan Review — supplementary reading on FX-swaps topic
problem:
Repeat the Ando decomposition with stressed inputs.

| Rate | Value |
|---|---:|
| USD OIS 3M | 4.20% |
| USD LIBOR 3M | 4.50% |
| EUR OIS 3M | 3.30% |
| EUR LIBOR 3M | 3.40% |
| α | +0.25% |

Compute (a) the FX-swap-implied USD rate from EUR; (b) the no-arbitrage upper bound; (c) the excess and its interpretation.
keyFormulas: FX-swap-implied USD rate from EUR = USD OIS + USD LIBOR-OIS + EUR LIBOR-OIS + α
Upper bound = USD LIBOR + EUR LIBOR-OIS

working: Upper bound = USD LIBOR + (EUR LIBOR − EUR OIS) = 4.50% + 0.10% = **4.60%**.

parts.prompt: (c) Excess over the upper bound and its interpretation.
parts.answer: Excess = 25 bp = α — dollar-funding stress beyond unsecured-market premia
working: By construction, the excess equals α: the residual dollar-funding stress that LIBOR-OIS spreads do not explain.

Ando's interpretation: α > 0 reflects 'demand for funding through the FX swap [that] was strong'. Empirically observed during the BNP Paribas shock (Aug 2007), post-Lehman (Q4 2008) and the European sovereign debt crisis (late 2011).

intuition: α is the bit of the dollar-funding stress that even arbitrage between the cash bond market and the FX-swap market cannot eliminate, because the arbitrage requires balance-sheet capacity — and balance sheet is itself in short supply in stress. Per Coffey/Kos/Verdelhan (2009): post-2008, this is no longer a free trade; it's a paid trade, and the basis prices the cost.

title: JPY/USD 6-month FX swap — negative interest differential
source: Lecture 8 (Syrstad note); CIP standard derivation
problem:
Spot **S₀ = 150 JPY/USD**. Interest rates: **r_JPY = 0.5% p.a.**, **r_USD = 5.5% p.a.**. Tenor: **6 months**.

Compute (a) the forward rate F via CIP; (b) the swap points; (c) state which currency appreciates forward and why.
keyFormulas: F = S₀ × (1 + r_quote × t) / (1 + r_base × t)   (USD = base, JPY = quote)
Swap points = F − S₀

parts.prompt: (c) Which currency appreciates forward, and why?
parts.answer: JPY appreciates forward, compensating the JPY lender for the lower JPY interest rate.
working: The lower-yielding currency (JPY at 0.5%) appreciates forward against the higher-yielding currency (USD at 5.5%).

Intuition: a JPY lender hands over JPY at spot and gets back fewer JPY per USD at maturity — they earn less JPY interest but more JPY-per-USD value at the back end. The two effects exactly offset in the no-arbitrage forward (CIP).

intuition: The sign of the swap points always reverses the interest-rate differential: the higher-yield currency depreciates forward by the differential. The mechanic is enforced by no-arbitrage — if it failed, you could borrow the low-yield currency, swap it for the high-yield currency, deposit, and swap back at the locked F for a riskless gain.

title: Basis-point spread to USD cost — quick conversion
source: Coffey/Kos/Verdelhan (2009) — order-of-magnitude basis costs
problem:
A non-US bank funds **USD 500m** synthetically via FX swap at a **60 bp** premium above the no-arbitrage CIP rate. Tenor: **90 days** (act/360).

Compute (a) the 90-day USD cost of the basis; (b) the annualised USD cost.
keyFormulas: Period cost = Notional × spread × (days / 360)
Annualised cost = Notional × spread

working: Compare to 25 bp pre-2008: annual cost would have been 1.25m USD — half the 2008-stress level.

intuition: Basis-point spreads on dollar-funding books look small per dollar but are on multi-billion notionals run year after year. A 60 bp basis on USD 500m is 3m USD/year — the kind of recurring drag that pushes European banks to reduce USD-asset books even after the immediate crisis subsides.

title: Hedged EUR bond → NOK floating margin
source: Lecture 9 (Syrstad) — full-hedge worked example
problem:
A Norwegian mortgage company funds NOK adjustable-rate mortgages by issuing a **5-year EUR-denominated covered bond at a 3.50% fixed coupon**, EUR 100m, hedging via:
• **EUR IRS** — receive EUR 3.50% fixed, pay EURIBOR 3M flat.
• **EUR/NOK CCBS** — receive EURIBOR 3M, pay NIBOR 3M + 15 bp basis (the basis is ADDED to the NOK leg the bank pays).

Mortgage assets earn **NIBOR 3M + 80 bp**.

Compute (a) the net NOK floating margin after the full hedge; (b) the net margin if the basis widens to 30 bp; (c) the net margin if the basis tightens to 0 bp.
keyFormulas: Net floating NOK margin = Asset spread over NIBOR − Liability spread over NIBOR
Liability spread over NIBOR (after hedges) = Basis paid on NOK leg of the CCBS

parts.prompt: (a) Net floating NOK margin with 15 bp basis.
working: Pay EUR 3.50% (bond) → IRS cancels with receive 3.50%, pay EURIBOR → CCBS cancels EURIBOR with receive EURIBOR, pay NIBOR + 15 bp.
Net liability cost in NOK terms: **NIBOR + 15 bp**.

parts.prompt: (b) Net margin if basis widens to 30 bp.
working: Liability cost = NIBOR + 30 bp; net margin = 80 − 30 = **50 bp**.
A 15 bp basis widening shaves 15 bp off the bank's margin — exposing the bank to basis-spread risk even though FX and rate risks are fully hedged.

parts.prompt: (c) Net margin if basis tightens to 0 bp.
working: Liability cost = NIBOR (flat); net margin = 80 − 0 = **80 bp**.
Zero basis is the CIP / theoretical no-arbitrage condition — bank captures the full asset spread.

intuition: Even a fully-hedged book retains BASIS-SPREAD risk: the cost of converting EUR funding into NOK depends on the cross-currency basis, which moves with global dollar-funding stress and EUR/NOK supply/demand. Norwegian banks issuing EUR covered bonds priced this risk into their funding plans after 2008; in March 2020 the EUR/NOK basis re-widened sharply, compressing margins on this kind of book.

title: Implied cross-currency basis from observed forward
source: Lefeuvre (2009) — basis swaps as a dollar-need signal; Lecture 8 CIP derivation
problem:
Observed market quotes (1-year tenor):
• **Spot S₀ = 1.10 USD/EUR** (USD per 1 EUR).
• **r_USD = 5.00% p.a.**
• **r_EUR = 3.50% p.a.**
• **Observed 1y forward F = 1.1135 USD/EUR**.

Compute (a) the CIP no-arbitrage forward F*; (b) the deviation of F from F* in pips and as an annualised basis-point spread; (c) state the sign of the implied cross-currency basis on the EUR leg and what it implies about USD funding.
keyFormulas: CIP: F* = S₀ × (1 + r_USD × t) / (1 + r_EUR × t)   (USD = quote, EUR = base; t = tenor in years)
Deviation in % terms ≈ annualised basis spread for 1y tenor
1 pip = 0.0001 in this quote convention

parts.prompt: (b) Deviation in pips and annualised bp.
working: For a 1y tenor, a ~22 bp forward dislocation corresponds approximately to a ~22 bp annualised cross-currency basis.

parts.prompt: (c) Sign of the implied cross-currency basis on the EUR leg, and interpretation.
parts.answer: Basis is NEGATIVE (≈ −22 bp) → USD scarce; synthetic USD borrowers pay a premium.
working: F < F* means the realised forward EUR is 'worth less' than CIP says it should be.

From the perspective of an FX-swap dollar borrower (lend EUR, receive USD now, pay back USD later for EUR back): they receive less EUR back at maturity than CIP entitles them to, i.e. the synthetic USD borrowing rate is ABOVE the no-arbitrage rate.
Equivalently, the EUR leg of a CCBS pays EURIBOR + (negative basis) ≈ EURIBOR − 22 bp.
Per Lefeuvre (2009) and Coffey/Kos/Verdelhan (2009): a more-negative basis is a textbook signal of dollar scarcity post-2008. Pre-2008 the basis hovered around zero (CIP held tightly).

intuition: The cross-currency basis is the FX-swap market's price for any deviation from CIP. Post-2008, sustaining the arbitrage requires balance sheet, and balance sheet is costly — so the basis can persist negative for years. Hui, Genberg & Chung (2011) document that each Fed swap-line expansion in 2008-09 visibly tightened the basis by 25-50 bp, which is direct evidence that the deviation was being arbitraged away by abundant balance sheet, not by a change in rate expectations.

title: Fed/ECB swap line vs synthetic FX-swap dollar funding
source: Hui, Genberg & Chung (2011); Baba, Packer & Nagano (2009); Lecture 9
problem:
At the peak of dollar-funding stress, a European bank can access USD via two routes:

• **Fed→ECB swap line**: ECB on-lends Fed-supplied USD to the bank at **5.25%** (= USD OIS 4.25% + 100 bp policy spread). Tenor: 7 days.
• **Private FX swap market**: implied USD rate = **8.10%** (Ando-decomposition with α at crisis levels).

Notional: **USD 50bn**. Day-count: act/360.

Compute (a) the 7-day USD interest cost on each route; (b) the 7-day dollar saving from using the swap line; (c) the annualised dollar saving (extrapolating the 7-day spread).
keyFormulas: Period interest = Notional × rate × (days / 360)
Annualised spread saving = Notional × (FX-swap rate − Swap-line rate)

parts.prompt: (a) 7-day USD interest cost on each route.
parts.answer: Swap line: 51.04m USD · FX swap: 78.75m USD

parts.prompt: (b) 7-day saving from using the swap line.

working: Per Hui/Genberg/Chung (2011): each Fed swap-line expansion in 2008-09 visibly compressed the basis by 25-50 bp, consistent with the order of magnitude here.

intuition: The Fed's swap-line architecture is a global liquidity backstop that puts a CEILING on the FX-swap-implied USD rate that non-US banks face. Without it, persistent α > 0 episodes (2008, 2011, 2020) would impose multi-billion-dollar annual deadweight costs across the non-US banking system. Per Baba/Packer/Nagano (2009), this is why European banks' acute stress at end-September 2008 was concentrated in the days BEFORE the swap-line expansion — and broke after it.

title: Basel III leverage ratio — backstop check
source: Basel III leverage ratio (CRR Article 429); Lecture 7 (Bank Regulation)
problem:
A bank reports **Tier 1 capital = 110** and **total exposures (on- + off-balance-sheet, no risk-weighting) = 4,500**.

Compute (a) the leverage ratio; (b) compare to the Basel III 3% minimum; (c) the additional Tier 1 capital needed to meet the minimum if exposures are unchanged.
keyFormulas: Leverage ratio = Tier 1 capital / Total exposures
Basel III minimum: 3% (G-SIBs face an additional 50% of their G-SIB CET1 buffer)

parts.prompt: (b) Compare to the Basel III 3% minimum.
working: The leverage ratio is the non-risk-sensitive backstop — it is independent of RWA, so it constrains banks even when their risk-weighted ratios look strong.

intuition: The leverage ratio is the answer to one question Basel I-II missed: what if the risk weights are wrong? It binds independently of RWA, so a bank that gamed RWA down via models still has to hold absolute Tier 1 against absolute exposures. In 2008 several European banks looked well-capitalised on RWA but ran 50× leverage on total exposures — exactly what the leverage ratio backstop now prevents.

title: Liquidity Coverage Ratio with stress add-on
source: Basel III LCR (CRR Article 411-428); Lecture 7
problem:
A bank's 30-day liquidity profile:

**HQLA (Level 1 only, no haircut):** 250

**Outflows over 30 days (run-off rates per Basel):**
• Stable retail deposits 1,000 × 5% = 50
• Less-stable retail 200 × 10% = 20
• Operational wholesale 300 × 25% = 75
• Non-operational wholesale 200 × 100% = 200

**Inflows over 30 days:** 80 (from contractually due loans)

Compute (a) the LCR under base run-off rates; (b) the LCR if a stress scenario doubles the retail run-off rates; (c) the HQLA shortfall to meet 100% LCR under stress.
keyFormulas: Net cash outflow = Total outflows − min(Inflows, 75% × Outflows)
LCR = HQLA / Net cash outflow ≥ 100%

parts.prompt: (b) LCR under stress (retail run-off doubles to 10% / 20%).
(c) HQLA shortfall to meet 100% LCR under stress.
working: Bank must monetise non-HQLA assets (sell into HQLA), reduce non-operational wholesale exposure, or extend retail-deposit term to qualify as 'stable'.

intuition: LCR is calibrated to a 30-day idiosyncratic-plus-market-wide stress; the 75% inflow cap stops banks from arguing themselves out of HQLA on the basis of contractually-due inflows that may not actually arrive. The structural lesson: HQLA must be sized for the stressed run-off, not the base case, because run-off rates rise WHEN HQLA is hardest to monetise.

title: Net Stable Funding Ratio — structural funding check
source: Basel III NSFR (CRR2 Articles 428a-az); Lecture 7
problem:
Apply standard NSFR ASF/RSF factors to a bank's balance sheet.

**Liabilities & Equity (ASF factor):**

| Item | Amount | ASF |
|---|---:|---:|
| Equity | 100 | 100% |
| Term deposits >1y | 200 | 100% |
| Stable retail <1y | 500 | 95% |
| Less-stable retail <1y | 200 | 90% |
| Operational deposits | 100 | 50% |
| Wholesale <6m | 300 | 0% |

**Assets (RSF factor):**

| Item | Amount | RSF |
|---|---:|---:|
| Cash | 50 | 0% |
| Level-1 sovereign bonds | 200 | 5% |
| Residential mortgages | 600 | 65% |
| Performing corporate loans | 350 | 85% |
| Other (illiquid) | 100 | 100% |

Compute (a) Available Stable Funding; (b) Required Stable Funding; (c) NSFR.
keyFormulas: ASF = Σ (Liability × ASF factor)
RSF = Σ (Asset × RSF factor)
NSFR = ASF / RSF ≥ 100%
intuition: NSFR is the long-leg complement to the LCR's short-leg: where LCR asks 'can you survive 30 days of stressed outflows', NSFR asks 'is your asset book funded by liabilities stable enough for the asset's maturity'. A bank that funds illiquid corporate loans (RSF 85%) with overnight wholesale (ASF 0%) fails NSFR — exactly the maturity-mismatch model that broke in 2007–08.

title: MREL stack — own funds + eligible liabilities vs requirement
source: BRRD MREL technical standards; BoE bail-in guide; Lecture 11
problem:
A bank's loss-absorbing stack:

| Item | Amount |
|---|---:|
| CET1 | 100 |
| AT1 hybrid | 10 |
| T2 subordinated | 20 |
| Non-preferred senior bonds (eligible) | 90 |
| **Total bail-in-able** | **220** |

**RWA = 1,000.** Pillar 1 = 8% RWA, Pillar 2 Requirement (P2R) = 2.5% RWA.

Compute (a) the bank's MREL ratio; (b) the SRB-style required MREL = LAA + RA, where LAA = Loss Absorption Amount (P1 + P2R) and RA = Recapitalisation Amount (P1 + P2R); (c) the surplus or shortfall.
keyFormulas: MREL ratio = (Own funds + Eligible liabilities) / RWA
LAA = (P1 + P2R) × RWA
RA = (P1 + P2R) × RWA   [SRB convention; jurisdictions vary on whether the CBR enters RA]
Required MREL = LAA + RA

working: Held 220 vs required 210 → **surplus of 10 = 1.0% of RWA**.

Important nuance: the Combined Buffer Requirement (CCB + CCyB + O-SII + systemic) sits on top of the MREL requirement and must be met in CET1 separately (the M-MDA threshold). If the bank has CBR = 4% RWA but only 100 of CET1, it may breach CBR-on-top-of-MREL even with the MREL surplus shown.

intuition: MREL = LAA + RA is engineered so a failing bank can absorb losses 'on the way down' (LAA writes off equity / converts AT1, T2, NPS) AND still re-emerge with enough capital to be a viable going concern (RA rebuilds CET1 to operating levels). Without RA, bail-in produces a recapitalised but immediately undercapitalised bank — defeating the purpose. The doubling of (P1 + P2R) is the structural minimum; the CBR layered on top via M-MDA enforces capital quality during normal times.

title: Capital constraint on balance-sheet growth
source: Lecture 7 (Bank Regulation); May 2024 Q2b grading guide
problem:
A bank reports **CET1 = 140**, **REA = 1,000** (CET1 ratio 14.0%, vs combined min ~10.5%).

Management wants to grow REA by **20% next year** while maintaining the same 14.0% target ratio.

Compute (a) the new REA target; (b) the CET1 needed to hold the 14.0% ratio; (c) the capital gap and at least three sources to bridge it.
keyFormulas: Required CET1 = target ratio × REA
Sources of new CET1: retained earnings; rights issue (new equity); reduced dividend payout; lower target ratio (within minimums)

parts.prompt: (c) Capital gap and at least three sources to bridge it.
parts.answer: Gap = +28; sources: retained earnings, rights issue, reduced dividend payout (or accept a lower target ratio)
working: 1. **Retained earnings** — most common; constrained by ROE and dividend policy. With ROE on RWA of 1.5% post-tax (15 of profit/year on 1,000 RWA) and 50% payout, retention ≈ 7.5/year → 28/7.5 ≈ 3.7 years to bridge.
2. **Rights issue / common equity issuance** — raise 28 directly from the market; instant but dilutive.
3. **Reduced dividend payout** — retain more profit; signal-sensitive (markets may interpret as distress).
4. **Lower target ratio** — accept e.g. 12% ratio: needed CET1 = 144; gap shrinks to 4. Constraint: must stay above combined min ~10.5% with a buffer for stress.

intuition: Capital is the binding constraint on bank balance-sheet growth. A bank that wants to grow assets must either: (i) grow CET1 in step, (ii) shed RWA to free capital (e.g. synthetic securitisation — see Set 1 securitisation questions), or (iii) accept a lower CET1 ratio (within minimums). This is why 'capital-light' growth strategies like off-balance-sheet conduits (Elmer 1999) became popular pre-2008 — and why the leverage ratio backstop now caps them.

title: Three-tranche CDO loss waterfall — three pool-loss scenarios
source: Gibson (2004), 'Understanding the Risk of Synthetic CDOs'; Davi (2008) tranche notes; Lecture 10
problem:
A CDO references a $1bn pool, tranched as follows:

| Tranche | Attach | Detach | Notional |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Equity | 0% | 3% | $30m |
| Mezzanine | 3% | 8% | $50m |
| Senior | 8% | 100% | $920m |

Compute the loss to each tranche under realised pool losses of (a) **$20m (2%)**; (b) **$60m (6%)**; (c) **$200m (20%)**. Express as both currency amount and as a percentage of the tranche.
keyFormulas: Tranche loss = max(0, min(Pool loss − Attach, Tranche notional))
Cumulative subordination protects each tranche by exactly the sum of junior-tranche notionals

working: Pool loss 20m is below the equity detach point of 30m.
Equity loss = min(20, 30) = **20m** = 20/30 = **66.67%** of equity tranche.
Remaining loss climbs into mezz: 60 − 30 = 30m absorbed by mezz = **30m** = 30/50 = **60.00%** of mezz tranche.
Remaining loss to senior = 200 − 80 = **120m** = 120/920 = **13.04%** of senior tranche.

intuition: Subordination is binary: a tranche either takes 100% of the loss in its band or none of it (until losses reach its attach point). This non-linearity is what makes mezz tranches 'fragile' — once attached, losses escalate fast — and what makes the senior look safe in unconditional EL terms but catastrophic conditional on extreme pool losses (Coval/Jurek/Stafford).

title: Attach/detach points from tranche notionals
source: Gibson (2004); RAM Synthetic CDOs primer; Lecture 10
problem:
A CDO references $1bn. Tranche notionals: equity **$40m**, mezzanine **$80m**, super-senior **$880m** (no separate AAA tranche).

Compute (a) the attach/detach points of each tranche as % of the pool; and the loss to each tranche under pool losses of (b) **$50m (5%)**, (c) **$100m (10%)**, (d) **$250m (25%)**.
keyFormulas: Detach[i] = Σ_{j≤i} Notional[j] / Pool
Attach[i] = Detach[i−1] (with Attach[0] = 0)
Tranche loss = max(0, min(Pool loss − Attach × Pool, Tranche notional))
intuition: The attach/detach grid is the only thing that determines tranche-level loss. For a synthetic CDO with thin equity (4%), even a moderate pool loss of 25% reaches the super-senior — exposing investors who thought they were buying a 'safer than AAA' instrument to material principal write-downs. This is the geometry behind the AIG super-senior debacle.

title: Expected loss on equity / mezz / senior under a discrete loss distribution
source: Coval, Jurek & Stafford (2009), 'The Economics of Structured Finance' (JEP); Gibson (2004)
problem:
A $1bn pool has the following loss distribution:

| Pool loss | Probability |
|---:|---:|
| 0 | 0.60 |
| 20 | 0.25 |
| 80 | 0.10 |
| 200 | 0.05 |

Tranches: equity **$30m** (0–3%), mezzanine **$50m** (3–8%), senior **$920m** (8–100%).

Compute (a) the pool's expected loss; (b) the expected loss on each tranche, in $m and as a % of tranche notional; (c) verify that the three tranche ELs sum to the pool EL.
keyFormulas: EL_tranche = Σ_s P(s) × max(0, min(L_s − Attach × Pool, Tranche notional))
EL_pool = Σ_s P(s) × L_s = Σ_i EL_tranche[i]

working: This is mechanical: every dollar of pool loss is allocated to exactly one tranche, so tranche-level ELs partition the pool EL exactly.

intuition: The senior tranche has only 0.65% EL — looks rock-solid in unconditional terms. But notice the conditional structure: the senior takes losses ONLY in the worst-case scenario (probability 5%), and CONDITIONAL on that scenario it loses 13% of notional. This is exactly the Coval/Jurek/Stafford 'economic catastrophe bond' point: same EL as a high-grade corporate, but losses concentrated in the worst aggregate states — where marginal utility is highest. Pricing it as a single-name AAA mispriced this systematic-risk loading.

title: AIG-style super-senior unfunded exposure
source: Gibson (2004); Lecture 10 (the AIG case); glossary entry 'aig'
problem:
A synthetic CDO references $1bn. Tranching: equity 0–3% ($30m), mezz 3–7% ($40m), senior 7–15% ($80m), super-senior 15–100% ($850m).

A monoline / AIG-style protection seller writes unfunded protection on the super-senior tranche (no IM posted at inception).

Compute (a) the pool-loss threshold above which super-senior takes losses; (b) super-senior loss at pool loss 12% ($120m); (c) super-senior loss at pool loss 25% ($250m), in $m and as % of SS; (d) explain why 'unfunded' is the structural risk in this setup.
keyFormulas: SS attach point in $ = 15% × Pool = $150m
SS loss = max(0, Pool loss − $150m), capped at $850m

working: SS attaches at 15% × $1bn = **$150m**. Below this, SS loss = 0.
Sub-tranches: equity 30 (100%), mezz 40 (100%), senior 50/80 = 62.5%; SS untouched.
Sub-tranches all fully wiped: equity 30, mezz 40, senior 80, SS 100. Sum = 250 ✓.

parts.answer: No IM posted at inception → counterparty exposure on AIG itself. AIG's downgrade triggered ISDA collateral calls (~$30bn by Sept 2008), not pool losses.
working: Funded protection (e.g. CLNs): protection seller pre-funds par at inception → no counterparty risk for the buyer.

Unfunded protection (CDS without IM): payment is contingent on AIG's credit standing. ISDA Master Agreements include CSAs with rating triggers — when AIG was downgraded in 2008, the triggers required AIG to post collateral retroactively across its book.

Per glossary 'aig' / Lecture 10: the cumulative collateral demand reached ~$30bn by mid-September 2008, exhausting AIG's liquidity and triggering the Fed's $85bn rescue. The losses were NOT yet realised pool losses — they were collateral calls on AIG's contractual exposure.

intuition: The super-senior tranche illustrates why a 'safer than AAA' label is not the same as 'free of risk'. Two distinct exposures stack: (i) tail pool-loss risk above 15%; (ii) counterparty risk on the protection seller — which is dominant when the seller is AIG-FP, levered 100×, with no IM posted, holding ~$440bn of CDS protection on senior tranches. The 2008 unwind was driven by (ii) not (i).

title: Money multiplier — and why BoE (2014) calls it 'incorrect but persistent'
source: Bank of England (McLeay, Radia & Thomas 2014), 'Money creation in the modern economy' — course reading
problem:
Textbook money multiplier:  m = (1 + c) / (rr + c), where rr = reserve ratio and c = currency-deposit ratio.

**Base case:** rr = 5%, c = 10%, monetary base MB = 200.

Compute (a) m and broad money M; (b) m and M if c falls to 5% (less currency held); (c) m and M if rr rises to 10%; (d) state the BoE (2014) critique and what actually constrains broad-money creation in modern systems.
keyFormulas: Broad money M = MB × m
BoE 2014: in modern systems, loans CREATE deposits; reserves accommodate ex-post.

working: Less currency leakage → larger money multiplier.
Higher reserve ratio → smaller multiplier (more reserves locked up per deposit).

parts.answer: The textbook story (deposits → reserves → loans) reverses the actual sequence. Loans CREATE deposits; reserves accommodate ex-post.
working: Per BoE (2014) 'Money creation in the modern economy': commercial banks do not lend out pre-existing deposits and they are not constrained ex-ante by reserves.

When a bank extends a loan it credits the borrower's account: a new asset (loan) and a new liability (deposit) appear simultaneously on its balance sheet — inside money is created by the credit decision, not by the reserve.

Constraints on broad-money creation in modern systems: **bank capital** (CET1 / leverage), **liquidity rules** (LCR / NSFR), **profitability** of marginal lending, **demand for credit**, and the **central-bank policy rate** (which influences loan demand and bank funding cost).
The reserve multiplier is a useful accounting identity but not a causal description of how money is created.

intuition: Both views co-exist in undergraduate textbooks — but the BoE (2014) view is the operational one. A reserve-multiplier story would predict that QE (huge increase in MB) directly multiplies into broad money — but post-2008 QE shows broad money barely budged because banks faced capital and demand constraints, not reserve constraints. Memorising m = (1+c)/(rr+c) is a useful identity; relying on it as causal logic gets the post-2008 macro wrong.

title: Diamond-Dybvig run scenario — welfare under a self-fulfilling panic
source: Diamond & Dybvig (1983), 'Bank Runs, Deposit Insurance, and Liquidity'; supplementary reading on liquidity-risk topic
problem:
Same project technology as Set 1's calc-dd-001 (100 depositors, 1 each at t=0; project pays **1 at t=1** liquidated / **2.25 at t=2** held to maturity; 40 D-types and 60 L-types) BUT for this question assume a simpler **symmetric utility u(C) = √C for both types** and a two-deposit contract calibrated to **C₁* = 1.30, C₂* = 1.80** (this satisfies the bank's break-even: 100 − 40×1.30 = 48 of project rolls at 2.25 to fund 60×1.80 = 108 ✓; the C₁*/C₂* values differ from calc-dd-001 because that question uses a different L-type utility specification).

Ex-ante welfare = 40·u(C₁*) + 60·u(C₂*).

Compute (a) the no-run welfare; (b) under a run (all 100 withdraw at t=1, bank can only liquidate the project at par 1, paying first-come-first-served), how many depositors are paid in full / partially / nothing; (c) the run-state welfare and the welfare loss vs no-run.
keyFormulas: No-run welfare = 40 √C₁* + 60 √C₂*
Run capacity at t=1 = total deposits × 1 (par liquidation) = 100
First-come-first-served: paid in full while cumulative payouts ≤ 100
Welfare loss = No-run welfare − Run welfare

parts.prompt: (b) Run scenario: how many depositors paid in full / partially / nothing.
parts.answer: 76 paid 1.30 in full · 1 paid 1.20 (partial, residual cash) · 23 paid 0
working: All 100 depositors withdraw at t=1; bank can only liquidate the project at par 1, so total cash available = **100**.
Number paid in full at C₁* = 1.30: floor(100 / 1.30) = **76 depositors** (total paid out = 76 × 1.30 = 98.80).
Residual cash = 100 − 98.80 = **1.20** → goes to the 77th depositor (partial payout).
Welfare loss = 126.11 − 87.75 = **38.36** (±0.1) — a 30% welfare destruction relative to no-run.

intuition: The run equilibrium is Pareto-dominated by the no-run equilibrium even under symmetric information — but each depositor's optimal action conditional on others running is to run too. Diamond & Dybvig's result: any of three policy devices (suspension of convertibility, deposit insurance, fully-credible LOLR) implements the no-run equilibrium under known π_D. With aggregate uncertainty over π_D, suspension fails and deposit insurance dominates — which is why DI became the global default and why Diamond, Dybvig and Bernanke share the 2022 Nobel.

title: Repo haircut, gearing, and the margin spiral
source: Krishnamurthy (2010), 'How debt markets have malfunctioned in the crisis' (JEP); Brunnermeier & Pedersen (2009)
problem:
A leveraged investor holds AAA structured-credit bonds funded entirely via overnight repo. **Equity = $20m**.

Pre-crisis repo haircut = **5%**. Crisis haircut = **30%** (per Krishnamurthy 2010 / Gorton & Metrick 'run on repo').

Compute (a) the maximum position size and gearing at each haircut level; (b) the forced sale required if the position was at the pre-crisis maximum and the haircut jumps to 30%; (c) describe the Brunnermeier-Pedersen spiral that this triggers.
keyFormulas: Position × haircut = Equity required
Max position = Equity / haircut
Gearing = Position / Equity = 1 / haircut

parts.prompt: (a) Max position and gearing at each haircut.
working: A 6× increase in haircut produces a 6× decrease in gearing — exactly because gearing = 1/haircut.

parts.prompt: (b) Forced sale if pre-crisis position was at maximum and haircut jumps to 30%.
working: Original position: $400m. New max at same equity: $66.67m.
Equivalently: equity must rise by (0.30 − 0.05) × 400 = $100m to maintain the position — impossible overnight, so the position must shrink instead.

parts.answer: Forced sale → price drops → measured volatility rises → haircuts widen further → more forced sales (margin spiral). Concurrent loss spiral if equity is also being eroded.
working: **Margin spiral (Brunnermeier-Pedersen 2009):** price falls → measured volatility rises → required margins/haircuts widen → trader's funding capacity falls → forced selling → further price falls.
**Loss spiral:** price falls → leveraged trader's equity falls → forced deleveraging → more selling → further falls. (At 20× gearing, a 5% price fall wipes out 100% of equity.)
**Empirical fingerprint (Krishnamurthy 2010 / Gorton-Metrick):** repo haircuts on structured collateral rose from ~0% to ~45-50% in 2007–08 — exactly the 6× kind of shift modelled here.

intuition: The 1/haircut identity is why funding-liquidity stress is non-linear in collateral conditions: a haircut moving from 2% to 8% (a small absolute change) corresponds to gearing falling from 50× to 12.5× (a factor-of-4 deleveraging). This is why the shadow-banking system unwound so fast in 2007–08 — the haircut adjustment is multiplicative on positions but is presented as a small percentage. Procyclicality of haircuts is one of the post-crisis Basel III reforms (countercyclical buffer, leverage-ratio backstop).
